extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, anatomists, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientists and observers)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and evaluating first-hand observational reports, book reviews, and practical procedures for natural phenomena (animals, anatomy, volcanology, salt-making) intended for a learned scientific journal. Emphasizes methods of observation, dissection technique, novelty/priority, and practical procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and priority of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the doctrine or experiments ... be new and unheard of; compare dates of publication and prior works to establish priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the dates of similar works (e.g., Boyle's New Experiments printed earlier) and examine whether the author consulted or received ideas from prior workers; do not accept claims of novelty without checking registers and prior publications. Anti-pattern: claiming originality while earlier printed works or records show prior exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution and record of consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should accurately report where they deposited manuscripts and whom they consulted (e.g., 'he commended his manuscript to the judgment of the Royal Society' — check register-books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify claims that papers were submitted to learned bodies; check institutional registers or the testimony of intermediaries (e.g., Sir Robert Moray). Misleading or unverified claims of having sought or received institutional review are grounds for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and completeness of experimental/technical description
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide precise construction and operational parameters (measurements, depths, bed dimensions, channels) so processes can be replicated or judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (salt-making): first receptacle water 20 inches deep; second receptacle 10 inches deep; salt beds 15 feet by 14 feet; water in beds not above 1½ inches. Include openings, channels, timing, instruments. Anti-pattern: vague or missing dimensions and steps that prevent assessment or replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of environmental variables and operational timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for weather, wind, rain, and timing when describing practical processes and their yields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (salt-making): stop openings during rain; the hottest years and windy conditions produce most salt; west and northwest winds best; drawing cream 4–5 hours before harvest improves table salt whiteness. Report how long processes take and how weather affects output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors determining product quality (salt whiteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three things to be considered for whiteness: first, earth of the marsh; second, make the salt with good store of water; third, the dexterity of the salt-man who draws it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: avoid letting earth at the bottom mingle with salt; draw the cream (top-formed salt) hours before main harvest to obtain whiter finer grains. Note trade-offs: adding more water may whiten salt but reduce yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and maintenance of production sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures for maintaining marishes/marsh beds from year to year and protecting them (e.g., overflowing to a foot height, strengthening ditches with stones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe seasonal preservation practices and infrastructure (ditches, stone reinforcements), and how proximity to sea or channels affects supply. Include contingency operations (emptying beds after prolonged rain) and constraints (only open certain channels at low tide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meticulous direct observation and repeated verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark exactly the ways of weaving/behavior, attend closely to an individual at work, repeat observations across kinds and times to confirm patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (spiders): observe thread production, note how a spider darts a thread into wind and is carried aloft; record differences among species and seasons; look for evidence (legs, wings) on threads as signs of prey capture. Anti-patterns: single anecdotal sighting without comparative or repeated observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and seasonal reporting of behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Record environmental and seasonal context for observed behaviors and structural features (e.g., summer vs winter differences in spider threads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note which individuals (young/old) are active in which season, the typical structure of threads in summer (many tangled locks) versus winter (single threads), and the likely contributors to large phenomena (large individuals and long passages in summer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and sufficiency of anatomical figures and representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures/cuts must be exact and complete; existing best figures may still contain faults and need additions to be perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine anatomical illustrations for omissions and errors; supplement with additional details where necessary. Anti-pattern: relying on standard figures without testing or adding missing structural information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissection methodology: examine parts in their natural state
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine and accordingly draw parts in that state in which they are found naturally, without at all forcing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not distort or force tissues during dissection; determine whether parts are actually joined or separated by observing them in their undisturbed arrangement. Record how prior operations may have changed the part's situation or connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissection methodology: track filaments/nerve threads through tissues
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue the filaments or threads of the nerves through the substance of the brain to see where they pass and terminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt difficult but precise techniques to trace nerve fibres through brain substance rather than relying on superficial cuts. This is necessary to judge claims about origins/terminations of fibres and to test anatomical theories (e.g., Willis, Descartes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid adherence to fixed dissection laws; adapt techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not bind oneself to certain fixed laws of dissecting each part; change methods when necessary to reveal true structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate with manifest proofs why alternate cutting or preparation methods yield better knowledge; be willing to develop new approaches tailored to the part under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward functional claims made without structural evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from confidently assigning uses/functions to parts of which the fabric/structure is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question magisterial statements about the use of parts when their structure is not well established. Test theoretical assignments (e.g., common sense, imagination, memory located in specific bodies) against dissection evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative and developmental sampling in anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissections and examinations should be made of as many heads as there are different species of animals, and different states and conditions of each kind; include fetuses and diseased brains to observe formation and changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative anatomy and developmental stages to reveal formation and structures not visible in healthy adult specimens. Diversity of samples is essential to a reliable anatomical history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two accepted paths to understanding a mechanism ('engine')
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the contrivance is discovered by the author himself, or it must be taken in pieces to the smallest parts and examined both severally and jointly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible obtain an authoritative account of construction; otherwise perform exhaustive dissection down to smallest components and analyze interactions. Use this as a methodological standard for claiming mechanistic explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for volcanic/field reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Record pre-eruption signs (dark skies, thunder, earthquakes), precise dates and progress rates, effects on towns, morphological observations (channels, sciarri), and sensory/quantitative details (ash columns heights, noises, temperature of water near flows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give chronological account (e.g., 'eruption took place on 11 March 1669'), report estimated advance rates (miles/day or furlongs/day), describe impacts (towns overwhelmed), characterize erupted materials, and include vantage/safety notes (observing from towers; distance limits to avoid danger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic sampling and classification of erupted materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and compare ashes, cinders, sciarri, sal ammoniac, and other minerals from multiple distances and locations around volcano to note differences in moisture, grain, and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify materials by where they were collected (top/mouth, 1 mile, 4 miles, 10 miles, skirts), describe physical properties (dry like dust vs moist vitriolate), and note which materials come from gutters or channels of fire versus crumbled deposits; record spatial distribution relative to eruption source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate practical usefulness and modern relevance of historical or classical opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether old or classical opinions (e.g., Hippocrates' chemical opinions) are of use in the modern improved state of a science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works not only on originality but on their utility to current practice and knowledge. Anti-pattern: reverence for ancient authority without testing against modern understanding.
